```{r setup, include = FALSE}
source("_setup.R")
library(bayesmokken)
```

Pupils sit in classrooms, patients attend clinics, employees belong to teams.
When respondents are grouped, two things change at once, and this vignette is
about both.

## Why clustering is not a detail

Respondents in the same classroom resemble one another more than respondents
drawn at random. An interval computed as though all 614 pupils were independent
therefore counts each one as carrying more information than it does, and comes
out too narrow. The remedy is a bootstrap whose sampling unit is the
*classroom*: whole classrooms are reweighted, and what happens inside a
classroom is left exactly as it was observed.

The second change is easier to miss and harder to undo. Once respondents are
grouped, **"the average" stops having one meaning.**

- The **respondent-weighted** coefficient gives every pupil equal weight. Big
  classrooms therefore count for more.
- The **equal-cluster** coefficient gives every classroom equal weight,
  whatever its size.

These are different population quantities. If class size is unrelated to what
you are measuring they nearly coincide, and the choice is immaterial. If large
classes differ systematically from small ones — informative cluster size — they
come apart, and the two answer different research questions. Neither is more
correct. But the software cannot know which you meant, so it refuses to guess:
`cluster_target` has no default.

## The data

```{r data}
data(classroom_wb)
str(classroom_wb, give.head = FALSE)
```

614 pupils in 30 classrooms answering six five-point items. It is fully
synthetic and built so that cluster size *is* informative, which is what makes
the choice of target visible rather than academic (see `?classroom_wb`).

```{r cluster-info}
items <- paste0("wb", 1:6)
bm_cluster_info(classroom_wb$class_id, data = classroom_wb[, items])
```

```{r fig-clusters, fig.alt = "Classrooms ordered by size, showing the weight each of the two population targets assigns to each classroom: respondent weighting rises with class size while equal-cluster weighting is flat."}
bm_plot_clusters(classroom_wb$class_id, show_targets = TRUE)
```

That figure is the whole argument in one picture. Under respondent weighting
the bars track class size; under equal-cluster weighting they are level.

## Declaring the supports

Polytomous items need their **support** — the response categories the
instrument defines — declared rather than inferred:

```{r supports}
sup <- bm_supports(classroom_wb, items = items)
sup[1:2]
```

This is required, not optional. The denominator of $H$ is a maximum attainable
covariance computed *at the declared support*. If a category was never used in
your sample, inferring the support from the data would quietly compute the
denominator at the wrong place and return a number that looks fine. So the
package asks.

`bm_supports()` reads the categories it can see; when the instrument defines
categories your sample missed, say so with `extend`:

```{r supports-extend, eval = FALSE}
sup <- bm_supports(classroom_wb, items = items, extend = 1:5)
```

## Fitting

```{r fit-resp}
fit_resp <- bb_mokken_h(
  classroom_wb[, items],
  item_type      = "ordinal",
  supports       = sup,
  cluster        = as.character(classroom_wb$class_id),
  cluster_target = "respondent",
  weight_law     = "complete_record",
  draws          = 2000,
  seed           = 1
)
fit_resp
```

Six arguments, each of which the package refuses to choose for you:
`item_type` and `supports` fix the denominator, `cluster` supplies the
grouping, `cluster_target` names the estimand, `weight_law` names the
bootstrap law (`"complete_record"` is what `"auto"` resolves to once a cluster
is supplied, so writing it out is a declaration, not a change), and `seed`
makes it reproducible.

The printed `raw` line is the percentile interval of the draws; the reported
interval is built from it as the next section describes, which is why the two
do not share a midpoint.

## Comparing the two targets

```{r fit-equal}
fit_equal <- bb_mokken_h(
  classroom_wb[, items],
  item_type      = "ordinal",
  supports       = sup,
  cluster        = as.character(classroom_wb$class_id),
  cluster_target = "equal_cluster",
  weight_law     = "complete_record",
  draws          = 2000,
  seed           = 1
)

bm_compare(respondent = fit_resp, equal_cluster = fit_equal)
```

The two differ by about
`r fmt_h(abs(bm_interval(fit_resp)$point_estimate - bm_interval(fit_equal)$point_estimate), 3)`
here. That gap is not error, and it will not shrink with more data — it is the
difference between two population quantities. Report which one you estimated.

> **Minimum interpretation contract.** This is a repeated-sampling CI for a
> fixed declared item set. The interval construction was validated for the
> scale coefficient only; item and pair intervals are uncalibrated. Landmarks
> are descriptive. The cluster target is substantive. The interval is
> computable for two or more clusters; the confirmation evidence covers 22 to
> 320 clusters, and the result says on which side of that range it falls.

## What the adjustment does

The complete-record bootstrap draws one Dirichlet weight per classroom and
recomputes $H$ under those weights. Its percentile interval tracks the
sampling variance of the coefficient, but with few clusters it comes out a
little too short. The reported interval therefore does two things to the
percentile quantiles $q_L$ and $q_U$: it **reflects** them about the point
estimate $\hat H$, and it **expands** the reflected errors by a factor that
depends on the number of clusters,

$$k_G = \sqrt{\frac{G+1}{G-1}}\;\frac{t_{G-1,\,.975}}{z_{.975}},
\qquad
\bigl[\hat H - k_G (q_U - \hat H),\ \hat H - k_G (q_L - \hat H)\bigr]
\cap (-\infty, 1].$$

```{r multiplier}
iv <- bm_interval(fit_resp)
c(k_G = iv$width_multiplier, clusters = iv$cluster_count,
  respondents = iv$n_complete)
data.frame(
  raw = c(iv$raw_lower, iv$raw_upper),
  reflected = c(iv$reflected_lower, iv$reflected_upper),
  reported = c(iv$lower, iv$upper),
  row.names = c("lower", "upper")
)
```

Both operations are visible in the object: `raw_lower`/`raw_upper` are the
percentile quantiles, `reflected_lower`/`reflected_upper` the reflected and
expanded endpoints, and `lower`/`upper` the reported interval after the
intersection with $(-\infty, 1]$. Here nothing crosses one, so the reflected
and reported endpoints coincide; when the upper reflected endpoint exceeds
one, `upper_intersection` is `TRUE` and the reported upper endpoint is one.

```{r fig-calibration, fig.alt = "Interval multiplier k_G against the number of clusters: above one, decreasing toward one, solid from 22 through 320 where the confirmation was conducted and dashed outside that range."}
bm_plot_calibration(mode = "clustered")
```

The multiplier is a prespecified function of $G$, not a constant tuned on
data: at $G = 22$ it is about 1.11, at $G = 30$ about 1.08, at $G = 320$ about
1.01, and it tends to one as the number of clusters grows. It depends on the
number of clusters, not the number of respondents, because it is the cluster
count that governs how far the percentile interval falls short.

## How many clusters

The interval is computable for any $G \ge 2$. That is a computational
requirement, not a recommendation: the confirmation of the clustered article
covered cluster counts from 22 to 320, and the fit records whether its count
lies inside that range.

```{r g-outside}
small <- classroom_wb[classroom_wb$class_id %in% levels(classroom_wb$class_id)[1:10], ]
fit_10 <- bb_mokken_h(
  small[, items], item_type = "ordinal", supports = sup,
  cluster = as.character(droplevels(small$class_id)),
  cluster_target = "respondent", weight_law = "complete_record",
  draws = 500, seed = 1
)
iv_10 <- bm_interval(fit_10)
c(G = iv_10$cluster_count, k_G = round(iv_10$width_multiplier, 4),
  validation_status = iv_10$validation_status)
```

Ten classrooms run, with `OUTSIDE_CONFIRMED_CLUSTER_COUNT` on the result and
a visibly larger multiplier. Report that status when you report the interval.

## The earlier procedure, kept as history

Version 0.9.0 of this package used a two-stage bootstrap that reweighted
classrooms *and then pupils within classrooms*, and narrowed the resulting
interval by $1 - 1.5/\sqrt{G}$. The clustered article's current version
shows why that was the wrong repair: the within-classroom stage adds variance
of the same order as the sampling variance itself, and no multiplier that
tends to one can remove it. The procedure is still available, so that results
computed with the earlier version can be reproduced, but every call says so:

```{r historical}
warned <- NA_character_
fit_old <- withCallingHandlers(
  bb_mokken_h(
    classroom_wb[, items], item_type = "ordinal", supports = sup,
    cluster = as.character(classroom_wb$class_id),
    cluster_target = "respondent", weight_law = "hierarchical_cluster",
    draws = 2000, seed = 1
  ),
  bm_historical_method_warning = function(w) {
    warned <<- class(w)[1]
    invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
  }
)
warned
bm_compare(complete_record = fit_resp, two_stage_historical = fit_old)
```

Same data, same seed, same target: the historical interval is built from
draws that are more dispersed and then shrunk about their midpoint, and it
carries its own method identifier so that the two can never be confused in a
table.

## The published analysis

The clustered article analyses the SWMDK data from the **mokken** package:
two scales, teacher support and classmate support, rated by pupils in
classrooms. The package's complete-record stream is the article's archive
stream, so the article's own seeds reproduce its intervals.

```{r swmdk, eval = has_mokken}
utils::data("SWMDK", package = "mokken")
teacher <- paste0("Item", 1:6)
fit_teacher <- bb_mokken_h(
  SWMDK[, teacher], item_type = "ordinal",
  supports = stats::setNames(rep(list(1:5), length(teacher)), teacher),
  cluster = as.character(SWMDK$classId), cluster_target = "respondent",
  weight_law = "complete_record", draws = 9999, seed = 1883301060
)
bm_interval(fit_teacher)[c("point_estimate", "lower", "upper",
                           "width_multiplier", "status")]
```

```{r swmdk-cached, eval = !has_mokken, echo = !has_mokken}
# The mokken package is not installed, so this section shows the cached fit
# instead. Install mokken to run it yourself.
bm_interval(bm_cached("swmdk_teacher_respondent"))[c("point_estimate", "lower",
                                                      "upper", "width_multiplier",
                                                      "status")]
```

```{r swmdk-both, echo = FALSE}
tea <- bm_interval(bm_cached("swmdk_teacher_respondent"))
cls <- bm_interval(bm_cached("swmdk_classmate_respondent"))
data.frame(
  scale = c("teacher support", "classmate support"),
  H     = c(fmt_h(tea$point_estimate), fmt_h(cls$point_estimate)),
  CI    = c(fmt_ci(tea), fmt_ci(cls)),
  row.names = NULL
)
```

```{r swmdk-cache-notes, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat("<p><em>", bm_cached_note("swmdk_teacher_respondent"), "</em></p>",
    sep = "")
cat("<p><em>", bm_cached_note("swmdk_classmate_respondent"), "</em></p>",
    sep = "")
```

The article reports the teacher scale at $H = .620$ with the interval
$[.576, .663]$ under the respondent target and the classmate scale at
$H = .592$, $[.556, .631]$, from 9,999 draws at the seeds used above. The
endpoints agree with the archive's to about $3 \times 10^{-13}$, the
difference being the order in which two implementations sum the same weighted
moments; the published-number gate (`inst/scripts/verify-published-numbers.R`,
run with `--published`) checks this against the article's own stored draws.
The visible notes above identify the stored fits, and the ordinary gate
runner's G-10 rebuilds and deep-diffs those caches from an isolated
current-source installation.

## Common errors

Each of these raises rather than returning something plausible.

**Missing supports on the clustered ordinal route.** A cluster argument makes
`item_type = "auto"` resolve to ordinal, but it never invents a support:

```{r cross-binary-missing-support, error = TRUE}
bb_mokken_h(srs, cluster = rep(1:25, length.out = nrow(srs)),
            cluster_target = "respondent", draws = 200, seed = 1)
```

**Explicit two-category clustered input.** Once its supports are declared, the
call reaches the path-crossing refusal: the clustered procedure was developed
and confirmed for genuinely polytomous items, not a relabelled binary scale,
and the refusal holds on every route.

```{r cross-binary-scope, error = TRUE}
binary_supports <- stats::setNames(rep(list(0:1), ncol(srs)), names(srs))
bb_mokken_h(
  srs, item_type = "ordinal", supports = binary_supports,
  cluster = rep(1:25, length.out = nrow(srs)),
  cluster_target = "respondent", weight_law = "complete_record",
  draws = 200, seed = 1
)
```

**Polytomous items with the independent-respondent law.** If you have clusters,
use them; if you do not, `bb_mokken_h()` has no records to reweight:

```{r cross-ordinal, error = TRUE}
bb_mokken_h(classroom_wb[, items], item_type = "ordinal", supports = sup,
            weight_law = "iid_respondent", draws = 200, seed = 1)
```

**Omitting `cluster_target`.** No default exists, by design:

```{r no-target, error = TRUE}
bb_mokken_h(classroom_wb[, items], item_type = "ordinal", supports = sup,
            cluster = as.character(classroom_wb$class_id),
            weight_law = "complete_record", draws = 200, seed = 1)
```

**A cluster vector out of step with the data.** `cluster` is matched by
position, so it must be as long as the data frame has rows and ordered the same
way. Subsetting the data without subsetting the cluster vector is the usual
cause, and it produces a silent misalignment rather than an error — check
`bm_cluster_info()` against what you expect.

**Singleton clusters.** A classroom with one pupil is a record of size one. It
contributes to the between-classroom variation like any other record, and
nothing inside it varies. `bm_check_data()` reports them; decide deliberately
whether they belong in the analysis.
